description: We are Team 404, building an interactive space mission design simulator that lets users create, test, and optimize mission architectures. By combining NASA data, engineering logic, simulation, and intelligent decision-making, our project helps users explore how choices in power, payload, communication, cost, mass, and risk shape mission success.
summary:
Team 404 developed 404: PATH NOT FOUND as an interactive Mars walk mission planner designed to help two astronauts explore Jezero Crater while managing terrain risks, robotic support, weather conditions, and limited habitat resources.

We wanted to answer a simple question: how can astronauts decide where to explore, what should be investigated by robots first, and when is it safer to return?

Our system combines NASA imagery, USGS elevation data, and historical Mars weather observations to build an interactive 2D and 3D environment. Astronauts select a survey region, and a simulated UAV first explores a cone-shaped approach corridor to prioritize the most relevant terrain instead of surveying a large area unnecessarily. The system then evaluates potential hazards, identifies science targets, and plans separate routes for the rover and astronauts using terrain-aware pathfinding.

We also introduced a persistent habitat simulation with 120 planned expeditions, resource tracking, weather-based equipment decisions, and a mission replay system that remembers previously explored sectors. Our 404-SVNet model evaluates whether to continue, avoid uncertain terrain, or scout first, alongside traditional routing algorithms.

The goal is not just to display Mars on a map, but to demonstrate how real terrain data, autonomous scouting, and resource-aware decisions can work together to make future Mars exploration safer and more efficient.
details:
Project Details

We built 404: PATH NOT FOUND because we wanted to understand what it actually takes to plan a Marswalk. Imagine two astronauts exploring Jezero Crater. Where should they go? Which areas are worth studying? What should the rover investigate instead? And how do we make sure everyone returns safely? Our project brings these decisions together into one interactive mission planning and simulation system.

Understanding the terrain

We started by developing an interactive Atlas using NASA and USGS datasets, combining HiRISE and CTX imagery, elevation data, MOLA/HRSC shaded relief, and THEMIS daytime infrared observations.

Users can select a survey region and choose scientific objectives, such as investigating unusual landform relief or surface texture. The system evaluates terrain risks using slope, local relief, and image texture, identifies potential science targets, and visualizes the results in an interactive 2D and 3D environment.

Why we chose a cone-shaped survey

Instead of surveying a large area immediately, we designed the UAV to investigate a narrow corridor near the habitat that gradually widens toward the selected science region.

Our reasoning was simple: why spend limited time and power surveying areas the astronauts may never visit? By prioritizing the approach and return corridor, the system focuses its initial scouting on the most relevant terrain.

If this approach does not identify enough reachable locations, the planner expands to a constant-width corridor and eventually a wider survey.

Planning the expedition

We designed the UAV, rover, and astronauts to have different responsibilities. The UAV performs initial reconnaissance, the rover investigates suitable ground targets, and the astronauts visit locations that meet their mobility and safety requirements.

Using terrain-aware pathfinding, including risk-weighted A*, the system calculates separate routes while considering slope, hazards, travel distance, and equipment.

Every crew expedition maintains a 20% return-time reserve. If simulated weather or unexpected hazards affect the route, the system can change the plan, withdraw the crew, or postpone certain objectives.

A habitat that remembers

We wanted the system to represent more than a single expedition, so we introduced a persistent habitat campaign with a goal of 120 EVA expeditions.

The habitat tracks limited resources, including oxygen, water, suit power, and robotic power. It also remembers previously explored sectors, identified hazards, visited targets, and mission outcomes.

This information can influence future expeditions instead of planning every mission from the beginning. Users can also replay missions to understand what happened and why particular decisions were made.

Weather and resource decisions

We integrated historical observations from NASA's Perseverance MEDA instrument and implemented a Theil–Sen trend estimator to provide short-horizon temperature scenarios.

Depending on the simulated conditions, the system can suggest additional equipment, such as heaters, cooling packs, or navigation beacons, while considering their resource requirements.

These scenarios use historical NASA observations as context rather than representing live Mars weather forecasts.

Testing 404-SVNet

We developed 404-SVNet, a machine-learning model that evaluates whether the mission should continue, avoid uncertain terrain, or send a robotic scout first.

We compared its decisions against traditional pathfinding methods using 300 held-out simulated scenarios. SVNet V2 achieved a return-probability Brier score of 0.089, while constrained risk-weighted A* achieved a higher mean utility of 52.22, compared with 40.72 for SVNet.

We included both approaches because we wanted to understand when machine learning helps and when conventional algorithms perform better.

How we built it and what we wanted to achieve

We developed the simulation, routing algorithms, and machine-learning components in Python, with an interactive interface built using TypeScript, React, Three.js, and OpenLayers. We also created a Windows desktop version combining the Atlas, 3D mission simulation, habitat management, and evaluation tools.

Our goal was not simply to build another Mars map. We wanted to demonstrate how real terrain observations, robotic scouting, mission planning, weather considerations, and limited resources could work together throughout an expedition.

The imagery and elevation come from published Mars observations, while scouting, hazards, weather scenarios, and mission outcomes are simulated.

404: PATH NOT FOUND is our attempt to turn Mars mapping into an exploration decision-making system, where finding a route is only one part of completing a successful mission.
